sections.b:
Ezekiel gives Tyre more space than any other nation but Egypt. Chapter 26 is the siege oracle, dated to the eleventh year (587/586 BC): Tyre cheered at Jerusalem's fall, and Nebuchadnezzar and then the sea itself are sent against it. Chapter 27 is a funeral song that makes the city a ship, built from the best of the world, loaded by about twenty trading peoples, and wrecked by an east wind. Chapter 28 has two speeches: to the ruler who says 'I am a god', and a lament for the king who was in Eden, the garden of God. Sidon gets a short word (28:20-23). Each speech closes with Tyre as 'a horror' that 'will be no more'.

Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city for thirteen years, according to Josephus quoting Menander. Ezekiel 29:17-20 admits that the army got no wages from it. Alexander took the island in 332 BC with a causeway, and the city was rebuilt afterward. How the oracles relate to these events is argued: see the notes at Ezekiel 26:12 and 26:14.

Ezekiel 27 is the Bible's longest list of Tyre's goods: metals from Tarshish, slaves and bronze from Javan, Tubal and Meshech, horses from Togarmah, spices from Sheba and Raamah, and wheat, oil and balm from Judah and Israel. Joel and Amos name the same trade as the crime: Tyre sold captives to Greece and Edom (Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:9-10). Ezekiel 28:16 says it filled the king with violence. Revelation 18 takes over the whole picture for Babylon the Great.

common: Many Christian readers see Alexander's causeway in 332 BC as the fulfillment of Ezekiel 26:4, 12, 14.
uncommon: Critical scholars note that Ezekiel 29:17-20 itself admits the Babylonian siege did not bring what 26:7-14 describes.

sections.h: The king of Tyre and the fall of Satan (Ezekiel 28:11-19)
sections.b:
The lament for the king of Tyre describes a being in Eden, the garden of God, covered with gems, a cherub on the holy mountain, blameless from the day of his creation until wrong was found in him, then thrown down and burned. Nothing in the poem names Satan. Christian readers from the early third century on (Tertullian, Origen, later Gregory the Great) have read it as the fall of a created spiritual being, and the Scofield Reference Bible teaches the reading. Others read the poem as a lament for a human king of Tyre, described in the language of an Eden story, as Zimmerli, Greenberg and Block do. Rashi, in the Sefaria text, reads a historical king, and Radak reads the Eden language as luxury. The Greek of Codex Vaticanus makes the cherub a separate being who leads the king out.

Churches that teach the fall of the angels rest it mostly on New Testament passages such as Luke 10:18, 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6 and Revelation 12:7-9. Whether Ezekiel 28 adds to them is the question. See the chapter page for the line-by-line reading.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 28:11-19; Isaiah 14:12-15; Luke 10:18; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6; Revelation 12:7-9

common: Many Christian writers since the early third century have read Ezekiel 28:12-19 as describing Satan's fall.
uncommon: Many modern commentators read the passage as a lament for a human king of Tyre and do not find Satan in it.

sections.b: Ezekiel uses Eden twice, both times of kings. In 28:13-14 the king of Tyre was 'in Eden, the garden of God', covered with gems, on the holy mountain. In chapter 31, Assyria (or Egypt) is a great cedar whose rivals are the trees of Eden, 'in the garden of God'. In both Eden is a place of glory from which pride brings a fall. Ezekiel's Eden has a mountain, jewels and a cherub, and has no woman, serpent or forbidden tree. Scholars read it as another form of the Eden tradition, as Ezekiel's own reshaping of Genesis, or as a Tyrian story turned against the king. In Ezekiel 27:23, by contrast, 'Eden' is a place in Syria (Beth-eden).

sections.h: A cherub on the mountain of God (Ezekiel 28)
sections.b: In the Hebrew of Ezekiel 28:14, 16 the king is 'a cherub, outspread, the one who covers', set on the holy mountain among stones of fire and later destroyed. 'The one who covers' recalls the cherubim whose wings covered the atonement lid of the ark (Exodus 25:20). The word 'outspread' (mimshach) can also mean 'anointed'. The Greek reads the same consonants as 'with the cherub', so that the cherub is a second being who finally leads the king out. This is a different picture from the four-faced cherubim of Ezekiel 1 and 10.

Ezekiel names seven nations in chapters 25-32: Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia (25), Tyre (26-28:19), Sidon (28:20-23) and Egypt (29-32); Mount Seir (35) is a further oracle on the usual count. The set is framed on one side by the end of Judah's own siege (24:1-2) and on the other by the arrival of the news that Jerusalem has fallen (33:21-22). The charges are mostly the way each nation treated Judah when it fell: gloating (Ammon, Tyre), contempt (Moab), revenge (Edom, Philistia). Babylon, the nation that actually destroyed Jerusalem, has no oracle in Ezekiel at all. Isaiah 13-23 and Jeremiah 46-51 both have one. Ezekiel treats Babylon as the LORD's instrument. The section ends with a promise to Israel (28:24-26) and, after Egypt, with the new heart and spirit of chapters 33-39.

Ezekiel speaks against Ammon twice. In 25:1-7 the charge is cheering when the Temple was profaned, the land laid waste and Judah exiled, and the sentence is that the people of the east will camp in Ammon's land, with Rabbah left to camels. In 21:28-32 the sword of Babylon is aimed at Ammon as well as Jerusalem. Ammon's king Baalis sheltered Ishmael after Gedaliah's murder (Jeremiah 40:14; 41:10).

Moab (with Seir, in the Hebrew) is charged with saying that Judah is no different from the other nations. The sentence is that its northern frontier towns, Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon and Kiriathaim, will be opened to the people of the east, along with Ammon. The Mesha Stele of about 840 BC lists Baal-meon and Kiriathaim among towns Mesha built.

Edom's charge is revenge against Judah, and the sentence reaches from Teman to Dedan. The oracle gives Israel itself the task of carrying out the LORD's vengeance. Ezekiel returns to Edom (Mount Seir) at length in chapter 35. Later Jewish writers used 'Edom' for Rome, and some readers connect the oracle with the Maccabean conquest of Idumea (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257-258).

The Philistines are charged with revenge 'out of an old hatred', and the sentence is that the Kerethites, the Cretan part of the coast peoples, and the rest of the seacoast will be cut off. The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in 604 BC.

The king of Tyre is covered with nine stones: carnelian, topaz, quartz, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, lapis lazuli, turquoise and emerald. These are the same Hebrew words as nine of the twelve stones on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17-20), with the order changed and the third row (jacinth, agate, amethyst) missing. The Greek of Ezekiel 28:13 has all twelve, in the order of Exodus, with silver and gold. The stones suggest a priest-king's dress, a garden of God, or the splendor of Tyre's wealth. Revelation 21:19-20 has twelve foundation stones for the New Jerusalem.

Ezekiel sends Tyre down to the Pit, to the lowest part of the earth, among the people of long ago and the ruins of old (26:19-21). He does the same for the ruler of Tyre (28:8) and sets the dead of the nations among 'the uncircumcised' in chapter 32. The deep that covers Tyre in 26:19 is the watery chaos of Genesis 1:2, now turned against a sea power. The contrast is 'the land of the living', where the LORD sets splendor.

Ezekiel does not condemn wealth in itself. Tyre's wisdom and trade gained real riches (28:4-5). The charge is that the heart grew proud over them (28:5, 17) and that trade filled the king with violence (28:16, 18). The ship of chapter 27 is full and heavy with glory, and the weight sinks her. Revelation 18 uses the same picture for Babylon.

The trade list includes 'human lives' (slaves) with bronze, supplied by Javan, Tubal and Meshech. Joel and Amos charge Tyre with selling captives (Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:9-10), and Revelation 18:13 ends Babylon's cargo list with the same Greek phrase for human lives.

Many of the trading partners of Tyre in Ezekiel 27 are names from the Table of Nations: Javan, Tubal, Meshech, Togarmah, Elishah, Kittim, Tarshish, Dedan, Sheba, Raamah and Asshur. Ezekiel uses them as live trading partners, not as ancestors. He lists Persia, Lud and Put as Tyre's soldiers (27:10), and names the same peoples again in the army of Gog (38:1-6).

Ezekiel is told three times to raise a qinah, a funeral song, over Tyre or its king (26:17; 27:2; 28:12). The form is the song for the dead, with its limping meter; the content is the opposite of comfort. The sailors who mourn in chapter 27 shave their heads and sit in ashes, as mourners did (27:30-31), and the dirge ends with the question 'Who was ever like Tyre?'
